t: Student Motivation Problems Crush the Kids, and They Crush Us, Too!
q: But here's the thing: when kids aren’t motivated to do work with care, the whole endeavor of education breaks down. - You can’t passively master anything, except passivity. For our kids to master art and science and mathematics and history, they’ve got to do work. And for that work to have its maximum impact, it’s got to be done with attention and focus and curiosity and engagement.

When teachers are faced with unmotivated kids, they get frustrated. One of the most painful things for an educator’s heart is to put work into lesson planning or paper grading or relationship building or curriculum mapping, only to find that their efforts are met with apathy or silliness or grade-mongering or complaint.

When teachers get frustrated, they quit — either fully or partially. I define quitting broadly. It’s not just when you put in your letter of resignation. It’s when you say, “Eh, yeah, that kid’s not teachable.” Or “Her home life is too rough.” Or “Whatever, it just is what it is — you can lead a horse to water, right?” When you quit, you stop growing.

Or sometimes, teachers respond to frustration with unsustainable overwork. This is what happens to many of our best people. They meet problems stemming from student motivation issues, and they respond with 80-hour weeks. Within a few years, they’re gone — used up like tissues.

When this is happening in my class, I look like a better teacher and feel like a better teacher and get results like a better teacher. And the best thing is that it's all sustainable — I’m not crushing my family or my health beneath the burden of overwork.

Value says, “This work matters to me.” Do you know many kids who are motivated by work that they view as totally pointless? Me neither. I know few adults like that, either. But when they do value the work, it’s so much easier for them to do. And the value belief is highly malleable at the classroom level.

But listen: student motivation is the problem behind our daily problems. The behavior issues in sixth hour, the low turn-in rates in fifth hour, the poor achievement in second, the grade-mongering in first — these all have the same roots.
x: Stuart argues that student motivation, though it sounds dull, is the problem sitting behind a teacher's daily problems, because when kids will not do work with care, education breaks down.
He draws a causal chain from unmotivated students to frustrated teachers to either quitting or overwork, to show motivation as a retention issue.
He draws a causal chain from unmotivated students to frustrated teachers to either quitting or overwork, to show motivation as a retention issue.

He traces a chain: passive students master nothing, unmotivated students frustrate teachers, frustrated teachers either quit in spirit or respond with unsustainable 80-hour weeks, and the best people burn out.
He claims the approach is sustainable because results improve without crushing a teacher's family or health under overwork.
He presents the five key beliefs of credibility, value, belonging, effort and efficacy as the core of motivation, each tied to supporting research such as Carol Dweck's work on mindset.
He argues that motivation is not another item on the plate but a lens that explains behaviour problems, low turn-in rates and grade-mongering across different hours.

t: How (and Why) to Ask Administrators for PD Funding
q: Unfortunately, much of this money is wasted. As Dan Weisberg of TNTP puts it, “We are bombarding teachers with a lot of help, but the truth is, it’s not helping all that much. We are not approaching this in a very smart way. We’re basically throwing a lot of things against the wall and not even looking to see whether it works.

The most powerful professional development of my career has almost always been selected for me, by me. It’s been attending local workshops with experts, or going to conferences, or reading books and studies in search of answers to my burning questions, or taking online courses from thinkers I respect. It’s the professional development I’ve received after standing back and asking, “What am I wrestling with? Why does it matter? Who might be able to help?

Survival Mode is antithetical to Flourishing Mode. If we want to flourish, we have to at some point carve out 20 or 40 or 60 minutes from the whirlwind and ask ourselves, “What would really help?” This’ll cost you an hour today and save you the next 180+ days on the job.

Many principals I’ve met are dying to have the “problem” of a teacher walking into their office and saying, “Hey, let me tell you how you can help me be awesome at my job.” If yours isn’t like that, it’s likely that inside of them there is that person who wants to be the kind of principal the delights in teachers owning their own development, but toxic stress has locked that person up behind a wall.

At the end of the day, it comes down to this: we’re professionals, not technicians. We’re like doctors and lawyers. Don’t tell me what society says — I don’t even know who “society” is. Ours is complex and professional and socially critical work. That means we need ongoing training to stay competent. Let’s act like it.

Second, find an expert who is offering professional development about that skill. It can be a book, or a course, or a conference, or some other newfangled thing. But find something that could help you move the work forward quickly in real life.

I’ve found in myself that right after a big ask, there’s a temptation to back pedal, to soften: “Of course, I might be able to just get by….” or “It’s probably too much money…” DON’T DO THIS. Just state your case, ask if you can sign up, and wait.
x: Stuart pairs the TNTP finding that PD dollars are largely wasted with the argument that the most powerful development is chosen by teachers themselves.
Stuart pairs the TNTP finding that PD dollars are largely wasted with the argument that the most powerful development is chosen by teachers themselves.

The second half is a practical script: pick one skill need within half an hour, find an expert resource, gather the facts on time and cost, craft the argument, request a short meeting and state the ask directly.

Stuart begins with the claim that US schools spend billions on professional development much of which is wasted, citing TNTP's Dan Weisberg, and argues that one remedy is teachers owning their own growth.
His central stance is that teachers are professionals like doctors and lawyers who need ongoing training, and that PD money is earmarked for exactly this purpose.

t: When You Need To Be A Mean Teacher
q: There is never a time when you need to be confrontational or intimidating.
Although it’s true that raising your voice and getting angry can quell misbehavior in the moment—because of a natural fear response—it’s never good for the long-term health of your classroom.
You see, when your students don’t like you (often secretly), trust you, or enjoy being in your class, then your consequences won’t matter to them.

Difficult students, and students with learning, social, emotional, or attention difficulties, in particular, are the most negatively affected. They tend to regress, shut-down, and stop caring altogether rather than make any lasting improvement.
Taking misbehavior personally, becoming vengeful, and showing displeasure is not only ineffective and remarkably stressful. But it’s childish.
You must hold yourself to a higher standard. You must rise above and refuse to get dragged into arguments or succumb to hurt feelings and petty grievances.
x: Responding to a recurring question about whether SCM ever calls for confrontation or intimidation, Linsin gives an unequivocal answer: no.
Raising one's voice may suppress misbehavior briefly through fear, but always damages classroom management over the long term.
Negative methods create dislike and resentment that weaken accountability, since students who don't trust or enjoy being around a teacher stop caring about consequences.
Difficult students and those with learning or emotional difficulties are described as most negatively affected by negative teacher reactions.

q: I've never met a teacher who didn't go into education hoping that they'd make a difference — that, ultimately, their work would promote the long-term flourishing of young people. There's no other way to begin talking about burnout than by starting with the ultimate aim of teaching: the long-term flourishing of our students.

So here's what few teacher books will tell you: great teaching is only possible when you are engaged with it with your mind and heart and soul, but this is hard because it's almost like present conditions were designed to rip out our hearts and drive us out of our minds and detach our souls. But our perception of present circumstances is malleable.

As a new teacher, I used to look down on older, burnt out teachers until I realized that none of them, years ago with newly minted teaching certificates in their hands, dreamed of one day becoming burnt out gripe-masters.

You will become proud; you will think you’re super amazing, God's gift to the profession. You will think you intrinsically merit greater attention than other teachers. You will expect to be honored frequently by the praise of others, and when others are praised instead of you, jealousy will sicken you like the stomach flu.

I went from the guy who fails mopingly to the guy who fails excitedly because of the lessons I was learning. It turned my worst days into some of my most productive; days in which my greatest weaknesses were laid bare like those nightmares where you realize you're not wearing any pants became days in which my strength as a teacher grew the most.

I didn't have time to think through all these things — she needed a response now. And this is why we have to cultivate our hearts — in moments like these, when there's no time for calculation, the basic orientation of our hearts comes forth from our lips; these tiny teacher decisions flow from who we are, so we have to do the work of making sure we are something worth flowing.
I'm not saying be a jerk to kids — I am saying you've got to have higher goals than to simply have them love you. Them loving you makes you popular, but not necessarily a good teacher.
x: A long essay on the inner work of teaching, in which Stuart starts from the aim of promoting students' long-term flourishing and lists four keys to an impactful career.
The essay ends by inviting readers to add their own tricks for tending the heart and mind from which teaching flows.
He urges teachers to detach self-worth from job performance, because success inflates pride and jealousy while failure turns a bad day into a bad self.

t: To the Teacher Who is Struggling Right Now
q: Being a teacher in the late fall can be tough. A friend of mine told me about one year when she went to see a therapist to help her process lots of bad feels late fall. Her counselor said, “Oh yeah. All y’all educators show up in the fall. Right around October, that’s when y’all start to roll in.

In education, the year is predictable. There’s this burst of optimism and energy and excitement in August. The first unit is often designed to be a high-interest win, for you and for kids. You’re teaching your classroom management plan, and you’re learning everyone’s names, and you have high, high hopes for all that you will accomplish together this year.

So then the internal messaging kicks in, and it’s either, “All right, I’m a terrible teacher,” or, “All right, my kids are broken, and I can’t fix them.” From here, we’ve got to either quit the work or internally disengage from it.

Ours is hard work. Maybe one of the hardest. We make a lot (thousands?) of decisions every day, and we infrequently get quick feedback on whether those decisions are the right ones. This demands so many skills, at such a high level, that it’s no wonder we often find the work difficult. So when we start feeling like we’re drowning each fall, let’s not be shocked. It’s to be expected.

If you don’t teach the youngsters how to live and to be and to contribute — how to flourish long-term — then your society has about a generation to go before all that’s left of it is a mention in the history books. We’re carrying a baton that’s been passed down to us over millennia. It is awesome and noble and beautiful to be a teacher. Circumstances might make that hard to believe, but nighttime doesn’t disprove the sun.

If it takes 70 hours a week to teach like you’re currently teaching, then you probably need to change how you’re teaching. “But Dave, I’ve got four preps, and they’re all new.” I understand that. So this means you’ve got to find ways to make those classes resemble one another. You’ve got to boil down the work that they require, thinking of lessons less like an artist thinks of making masterpieces and more like a coach thinks of making practices. Start with the constraint — set rules for yourself for when you will and won’t work. Figure out how to make work work from there. Trust me — it helps.

If you’re in the first five years of your career, give yourself lots of grace. Teaching is freaking hard. Most experts (e.g., Linda Darling-Hammond’s Empowered Educators, or Marc Tucker’s Top Performers blog at EdWeek) don’t think that the way we recruit, train, and retain teachers in the USA works very well. Just focus on becoming good at a few things — like six of them. This changed my career.
x: Stuart tells struggling teachers they are not weird or unfit, using the predictable rhythm of the school year and the therapist's remark about educators arriving each October.
Stuart tells struggling teachers they are not weird or unfit, using the predictable rhythm of the school year and the therapist's remark about educators arriving each October.
He traces how powerlessness snowballs into the two destructive stories, I am a terrible teacher or my kids are broken, which lead to quitting or inner disengagement.
He argues the work's difficulty is expected, given thousands of decisions with slow feedback, and its importance real, because societies that fail to teach their young do not last.
Written for the late-fall slump, this is a letter of encouragement to teachers who are struggling for any of a long list of reasons.

He gives concrete counsel: do not take hurtful remarks personally, reduce a 70-hour week by making preps resemble one another and thinking like a coach planning practices, and take a full day off weekly.

He offers a different set of reminders to move from powerless to empowered: the work is hard and important, hurtful comments say more about the speaker, teachers may need to work less, and a weekly day off helps.

t: How To Avoid Losing Your Students’ Attention https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2018/11/10/how-to-avoid-losing-your-students-attention/
q: As attention starts to wane . . . Eyelids droop. Fingers tap. Bodies sigh. . . . the teacher will speed up their instruction.
But this is a big mistake—because it only makes things worse.
The urge to rush and get done quickly will inevitably cause you to gloss over details, which are the most important element in making your lessons interesting.
Talking faster is a sure recipe for excitability, which is one of the biggest causes of misbehavior.
Speeding up acts as a triggering mechanism. It signals to students that you’re wrapping it up, which causes them to move on mentally, and sometimes physically, to the next activity.
When you notice attention waning—or, better yet, to avoid ever losing your students’ attention—slow down and focus on details .
They’re compelling and fascinating and pull students so deep into the lesson that they forget where they are.
x: Speeding up instruction when student attention wanes is identified as a common but counterproductive teacher instinct.
Linsin identifies a common teacher instinct—speeding up instruction when attention starts to wane—as a mistake that makes things worse.
Rushing makes lessons boring by causing teachers to skip the details that make content interesting and easier to follow.
Talking faster also triggers excitability, a major cause of misbehavior, and signals to students that it's time to mentally move on.

The recommended fix is the opposite of rushing: slow down and add more specific, granular detail when attention starts to fade.

t: The Five Key Beliefs: More than Band-aids
q: Teaching strategies are kind of like band-aids for teachers. For some teacher troubles, band-aids are perfect:

Band-aiding them seems to help today, but over time it burns us out because the problems are always popping up in new ways, all year long. We feel like we’re constantly chasing student motivation, following the lead of its latest symptoms but never, after those first few days of school, actually getting in front of it.

It’s fun when you give kids learning experiences that they actually take advantage of. It’s fun watching kids grow and learn and advance themselves down the road of mastery. We can taste and see that our work matters.

The trouble is that the older our students get, the more likely they are to be disengaged or bored or otherwise demotivated by school. At some point, they reach an age where they’re making judgments about school, constantly, asking themselves a few basic questions in every academic situation they find themselves in.

It’s not the assignment or the grading system or the curricular approach or the teaching style that makes kids do the work and do it with care. When you dig all the way down, it’s these five key beliefs:

And those things, the research says, are incredibly malleable. For example, our colleagues at the Chicago Consortium for School Research found in a survey study that students can go from believing those five key beliefs in a first hour class, and then in a second hour class believing almost none of them.
x: The implication is that teachers should understand the beliefs underneath behavior before reaching for new strategies.
Chasing the latest symptom leaves teachers burned out, stuck in complaint cycles, or counting the days to break.
The answers form five operational beliefs (Credibility, Value, Belonging, Effort, Efficacy), and these, more than assignments or teaching style, drive whether kids do the work.
He defines the goal as getting students to do work with care, then locates the root cause in five beliefs students silently test in every academic situation.
The answers form five operational beliefs (Credibility, Value, Belonging, Effort, Efficacy), and these, more than assignments or teaching style, drive whether kids do the work.
Citing Chicago Consortium research, he notes these beliefs are highly context-dependent, so they can differ sharply from one class hour to the next.

t: Why Allowing Your Students To Talk Can Be An Effective Classroom Management Strategy
q: It’s common to assume that allowing students to talk to whomever they want about whatever they want is a bad thing.
But when you decide when and how it’s done, it’s nothing of the sort.

Because it effectively releases the natural tension that builds up from sitting and concentrating for long periods of time. It relieves antsiness, restlessness, and excitability, which are major causes of misbehavior.
For most students, talking and sharing with friends is the quickest way to get boredom out of their system. It clears the boards, gets the blood flowing, and frees them to focus on the next lesson.

It shows them that you know what it’s like to be in their shoes and to sit, listen, and learn for an entire school day. It’s this kind of empathy that makes students want to please you and behave for you.
The key to allowing talking breaks is for you to decide when and how they’re done. It’s to teach and model precisely what is and isn’t okay before putting them into practice.
x: Allowing talk demonstrates empathy, which students appreciate and which triggers the SCM principle of reciprocity.
Linsin challenges the assumption that allowing students to talk freely wastes time or invites misbehavior, arguing instead that teacher-controlled talking breaks are an effective management tool.
Talking breaks release built-up physical and mental tension from extended sitting and concentrating.
A short talking break clears student boredom and 'checked-out' energy so they return more attentive to instruction.
Allowing talk demonstrates empathy, which students appreciate and which triggers the SCM principle of reciprocity.
The strategy only works if the teacher decides when and how breaks happen, with expectations explicitly taught and modeled first.

t: Linking My Past Burning Questions with Real Kids
q: What's the point of school? It's the long-term flourishing of kids. Our work is to promote that flourishing.

So what? This question has helped me relate things like literacy or argument or student motivation to diverse groups of teachers around the country. This is the common ground that all departments and subject areas and grade levels share. From this common ground, productive PD or strategizing or change can happen.

What's the best way to have kids master school and its material? Ultimately, there's no way to do this unless kids 1) do work and 2) do it with care. This means taking notes, asking questions, completing assignments, engaging with projects, writing essays, conducting research, turning in homework — the gamut. If you don't do work carefully, you don't grow. At anything.

What's the best way to help all kids do work with care? Create classrooms and policies and schools and assignments that cultivate the five key beliefs beneath student motivation. Blessedly, these beliefs are highly malleable, even in situations where students come from hard home situations or belong to marginalized groups.

First of all, these kids — about 4% of my total roster — are all delightful to teach at the macro level. Sometimes they're a challenge to teach — some more frequently and intensely than others — but when you zoom all the way out, this year I find, yet again, that it's a lovely job. I cherish these kids and am thankful that they are alive, and I do hope and pray that my work promotes their long-term good.

Second (and more to the point), the burning questions and answers at the top of this post become real and meaningful when applied to these actual kids. The kids are the place where theory ends and “sleeves rolled up” work begins.

How do I help more departments, teams, and schools to “get on the same page” and “row in the same direction” when it comes to long-term flourishing, teaching toward mastery, and maximizing the five key beliefs? After all, the more people in a school that you have doing this work, the better off all the kids will be.
